title: How Do Animals Survive 7 Months Frozen Solid?
description:
How do animals survive being frozen solid? Wood frogs freeze with no heartbeat for months, Arctic ground squirrels supercool below zero, Antarctic fish make antifreeze proteins, and tardigrades dry out and wake up decades later.

Sources:
https://www.audubon.org/news/frogs-freeze-survive-alaskan-winter
https://uaf.edu/centennial/uaf100/ideas/frozen-squirrels.php
https://phys.org/news/2016-02-animals-revived-frozen-state-years.html

Animated in the Claymation Set style.

topic: How do animals survive being frozen solid?
script: Frozen solid for seven months. No heartbeat. No breathing. You'd be dead. This frog just hops away in spring. So how do animals survive being frozen? Today, four champions of the cold, each with a totally different trick. Meet the wood frog. It lives as far north as Alaska, and it doesn't hide from winter. It just lies down under the leaves, and lets the ice come. The problem with freezing is sharp ice crystals. If they grow inside a cell, they rip it apart like tiny knives. So the frog plays a clever game. As ice touches its skin, its liver floods the body with sugar, up to ten times the normal amount. That sugar soaks into every cell, like a syrup that won't freeze. So the ice can only grow outside the cells, in the spaces in between. Up to sixty percent of the frog turns to ice. No heartbeat. No breath. In Alaska, it can stay like this for as long as seven months. Then spring comes, the ice melts, and the heart starts beating again. Our second champion uses the opposite trick. The Arctic ground squirrel never freezes at all, even when its body drops below zero. Scientists measured one at almost minus three degrees, the coldest body ever found in a mammal. How? It's called supercooling. Water needs a tiny seed to start freezing, like a speck of dust, or a bit of ice. The squirrel's blood is so clean, there's nothing for ice to grow on. So it stays liquid, below freezing. But that's risky. So every few weeks, the squirrel shivers, warms itself back up for a little while, then drops back into the deep cold. Now, dive under the Antarctic ice. The sea here is almost minus two degrees, cold enough to freeze most fish solid. But these Antarctic fish swim around just fine. Their blood is full of antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks in, the proteins grab onto it, and wrap it up so it can't grow. One of their cousins, the icefish, went even further. Its blood has no red cells at all. It's clear, like water. And then there's the toughest of them all. The tardigrade, or water bear, smaller than a grain of sand. When things get bad, it dries itself out, curls into a tiny ball called a tun, and basically pauses its life. In nineteen eighty three, scientists collected moss in Antarctica, and kept it in a freezer at minus twenty. Thirty years later, they thawed it out. Two water bears woke up, and one of them went on to lay nineteen eggs. So why do scientists care? Because we can't do this yet. A donor heart on ice only lasts about four to six hours. Researchers are studying the frog's sugar, and the fish's antifreeze, to keep organs alive for much longer. Four animals, four tricks: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, and drying out. Which one would you pick? Next time, how did a bitter bean become the world's favorite treat, chocolate?
key_facts: Wood frogs: up to ~60% of the body freezes, heart and breathing stop, glucose up to ~10x normal acts as a cryoprotectant; in Alaska up to ~7 months frozen (Audubon)
Arctic ground squirrel: supercools to about -2.9 C, lowest body temperature recorded in a mammal; rewarms every few weeks (UAF)
Antarctic notothenioid fish: seawater about -1.9 C, antifreeze glycoproteins bind ice crystals; icefish have no red blood cells / hemoglobin, colorless blood (Wikipedia: Antarctic fishes)
Tardigrades: moss collected in Antarctica Nov 1983, stored at -20 C, thawed 2014; two revived, one laid 19 eggs (phys.org 2016)
Donor hearts are typically kept on ice for about 4-6 hours
